Git and AI tools
Three of you asked for it:

When to use an AI assistant, and when not
Testing and collaboration on GitHub when an agent writes the code
How to declare the use of AI tools in research


The foundation we learn in the full course (two sessions of 2 hours) prepares you for our Agents for Scientists workshop, where we invite an agent, such as Claude Code, to work with us.


Block 09:30 to 09:40, last slide of it. 25 of the 27 answers name at least one AI tool in use. The three asks are grouped from the open answers, no quotes.

My turn I show something on my screen. You watch and type nothing.
Our turn We do the same step at the same time, I on my screen, you on yours.
Your turn You work on a task, with your neighbour. I help where it sticks.

Things may go wrong here. Everything we do today can be undone.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What is a commit?
A commit is a saved state of your files, with four pieces of information:

Who made it: a name and an email address
When: date and time
What changed: line by line
Why: the message you write with it


Block 09:45 to 09:55. Key words only, then the traces in a real repository on the next slide.

title: Git for Scientists

My turn The commits of the workshop website:

9 November: pre-work steps 1 and 2
15 November, a Sunday, 22:00: steps 3 to 5
17 November: step 6
19 November, the day before: these slides, 19 commits


At what times of day did Lars prepare this material?



Git forgets nothing. 34 commits until last night: 19 of them yesterday, 7 at 22:00 or later.



Block 09:45 to 09:55. The repository is public: gitforsci-rdc/website. No browser needed, the slide carries it. Git forgets nothing: that is the use of it, and it is the reason to choose what goes into a commit. The history shows that my instructions came late. This returns at 10:55.

Pictures: Lars Schöbitz, CC BY 4.0. K is Kim, R is Robin. Dashed: only on the laptop.


Block 09:45 to 09:55. Kim creates the repository on GitHub. Kim and Robin clone: three places, the same state. Laptops never talk to each other directly, always through GitHub. Words: local is the laptop, remote is GitHub. Clone once. A second clone is a second copy on the same laptop, and the two get mixed up.

Commit

Block 10:20 to 10:30. One pass, about 5 minutes, and say these out loud: 1. You cloned workshop in Step 5. Do not clone it again. Current Repository, workshop. 2. Current Branch, New Branch. The button at the bottom left must end in “to people-your-username”. If it ends in “to main”, you are on the wrong branch. 3. In Finder or Explorer: gitrepos/teaching-username, copy the one file, paste into gitrepos/workshop/people. 4. Changes shows one file with a tick. 5. Publish branch. 6. Preview Pull Request, then Create Pull Request at the bottom right. The browser opens. Fill in the two lines. On the right, Reviewers: larnsce. The room does not type here. Open the page Add your file on the workshop website.

Request larnsce as the reviewer.



I read every pull request that is open by Friday 4 December and write one question on it.


In the full course you do this in the room, right after the break. I walk the room and check in with each person. Online, I visit each break-out room.


Block 10:20 to 10:30, last slide before the break. About 30 minutes at home. In the room it is the first activity after the break with real learners: it gives me the time to walk the room and take questions one to one. The course is built in two sessions with time between them to practise. Today is the first session only. In the second session pairs review and merge each other’s work, 30 minutes of it; it is the part I would never cut from a full course.

Block 10:55 to 11:00, this slide and the next, while the synthesis of activity 1 runs. Everything you used this week is a repository. One sentence per row. The survey is a small app with its answers in a database. One course organisation on GitHub for you, one for the material, one for the administration. The point: the workshop teaches the tool it is built with, and every step you took left a trace I could see without asking.

Your preparation, in counts

Friday 20 November, 07:00. Four emails from me.


27 answered the survey


26 joined the organisation


17 ticked all five boxes


17 made a commit from the laptop



On Tuesday at 15:00 the last two numbers were 7 and 2. Most of the work happens in the last hours, this time also because my instructions came late.


Block 10:55 to 11:00. Counts only, no names, no chart of who worked when. Say that the pre-work decided who could type today.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What you wrote
Your notes from activity 1, grouped. I switch to the second tab.

Read it with your neighbour: which point surprises you?


Then the floor is open, for what you wrote and for your questions.


Block 11:00 to 11:10. Switch to the browser tab with live.html: it shows the result after the skill ran. Give the room a minute to read. Read one theme per row from each column out loud, then open it: who wants to say more on a point under What can be improved? Questions from the frame Parked questions fit here too. If the synthesis failed: open the board itself and read three notes per cell. Do not defend, say thank you and name one thing I will change.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Six things I do

Words I leave out: just easily quickly
Design for the novice: every click is written down
Know the learners, then design: survey first, content last
A learner account: every demo ran as rainbow-train
Type with the room, mistakes included
Try out new things: today the board and its synthesis


Each one has a slide of its own at the end of this deck.


Block 11:10 to 11:15. One sentence per point, each with its example from this morning. Clicks are usually written down with screenshots, which are missing this time. The content of today was written yesterday. Found one of the three words on my slides or in the pre-work? Park it on the board, I fix it in a commit after the workshop.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What motivates adults to learn





Self-efficacy: I am in control of my own life.
Utility: This will help me meet my goals.
Community: People I know are learning this with me.



This morning: a repository of your own, your own three lines, a neighbour.




Figure and wording: Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together, slides on motivation, CC BY 4.0. Art from openclipart.org.


Block 11:15 to 11:20, this slide and the next. Motivation is the strongest predictor of whether an adult learns something.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What takes motivation away



Unpredictability: what I do does not seem to affect the outcome.
Unfairness: the teacher plays favourites.
Indifference: nobody cares. A question in an issue stays without an answer. The material was last touched two years ago.






Which of the three do your learners meet most often?



Figure and wording: Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together, slides on motivation, CC BY 4.0. Art from openclipart.org.


Block 11:15 to 11:20. A push that is rejected without a reason I can read is unpredictability. An instructor who answers only the fast people is unfairness. Indifference is also: nobody notices that you fell behind in the pre-work. Ask for one hand per heading. One moment of my own if there is room: a course where the setup failed and the instructor went on.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
The full course







Session 1, 2 hours
What you saw today, and your own pull request in the room


Two weeks between
A repository of your own, with me as reviewer. Practice in a game with quizzes. A glossary.


Session 2, 2 hours
Pairs review and merge. A merge conflict. Working together: tasks and projects, organisation and profile.




Today you saw half of session 1.


Block 11:20 to 11:25, with the next two slides. The two weeks are where people learn it: they bring a project of their own and I review it. The game and the glossary exist in German so far, from the course of Tuesday: gitklar.ch/spiel. An English glossary for this website is in work.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Also on my list

Peer instruction: people explain to each other and review each other’s work. It is the pull request in pairs that you did not do today.
A place for questions, and the plain statement that a short workshop does not answer all of them.
Online: a short visit to each break-out room.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Where this comes from

Ten quick tips for teaching programming, Brown and Wilson, 2018
Teaching Tech Together, Greg Wilson, free to read
The Carpentries Instructor Training, open material and a certification


If you teach a technical tool, take an instructor training.


Block 11:20 to 11:25, last slide of it. It is the best use of your time, out of respect for the time your learners give you. My own route was the RStudio instructor certification in 2020, built by Greg Wilson on the same material; it changed how I teach novices. The Carpentries training is the open route today.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Would you teach this?
Your turn I would like to offer a workshop for people who teach Git: this design, its scripts and its material, for your own groups.

In your-username.md, add one line, then commit and push:
- Teach the teachers: yes / maybe / no. What I would need:
If you like, a second line:
- A moment in a course that took my motivation away:


 

Your answer commits you to nothing.


Block 11:25 to 11:30, with the last slide. The step of 10:00, this time alone. The second line is a choice: unlike a note on the board, a commit carries your name. No laptop setup: a note under Parked questions. The form of the offer is open; the answers shape it. They arrive as commits, which I can read with the tracker.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Words I leave out
just   easily   quickly

They say that a step costs nothing. A learner who is stuck on it hears: it is me.
This morning: look for one of them on my slides or in the six steps of the pre-work. Found one? Park it on the board.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. If someone finds one, thank them and fix it in a commit after the workshop.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Design for the novice

Assume that people know nothing about the tool.
No gap between two steps: every click is written down, usually with screenshots. They are missing this time.
Extra material for people with experience, marked as extra.


This morning: six pre-work steps with every click. “A button is a command” was the extra for those who use a terminal.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. The pre-work is where the novice design lives: a first-time user went from no account to a pushed commit in about an hour.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Know the learners, then design

A survey before anything is written: 27 answers decided the software.
A tracker shows who is where in the pre-work, without asking anyone.
The content of today was written yesterday, from what I read in the pre-work.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Most learners do the pre-work on the last day, and I teach better from what I read then than from a plan made weeks ago. It takes practice, and trust in the method, to walk into a room with slides that are one day old. The method is fixed (My turn, Our turn, Your turn, pairs, a learner account), the content moves with the group. Next slide: one choice the survey led to.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Why GitHub Desktop?


11
RStudio


6
GitHub Desktop


4
Positron


5
no preference



I chose against the largest group. For novices, RStudio is too much on top of Git unless I teach R and Quarto alongside.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Half of the room does not write code in R, and 10 of you do not use Git today. GitHub Desktop needs no programming language, and its buttons carry the names of the commands. I learned it in earlier workshops. The honest version: the choice has a cost for the 11.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
A learner account

Every demo this morning ran as rainbow-train: a second account with the rights you have, on the screens you see.
With my own account I am an owner. Buttons differ, warnings never show.
The account found the rejected push with the real email address before you did.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Costs one free account and one more browser profile.

title: Git for Scientists
section: Type with the room, mistakes included
text:
Type with the room, mistakes included

Participatory live coding: I type, you type, nothing is pasted.
A demo in two passes where time allows: once without stopping, once slowly.
A mistake on my screen is a moment to take apart together.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Then the next slide: the mistakes of Tuesday, and what they changed for today.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Try out new things

I used a Miro board for the first time, because Claude can now set it up for me.
The synthesis of your notes was a trial.


Inspire yourself and your learners with novelty, and learn new things along the way.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Say it at point six of the slide “Six things I do”.

13 pull requests in two hours
Three clones on one laptop: “clone once” is now in Step 6
A copied repository folder: today you copy one file

Too many emails before the workshop


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. The second cohort stays unnamed. Each line is a change you met this week: the instructions you followed are three days old.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
About 25 minutes. Due by Thursday, 19 November 2026, and at the latest Friday, 20 November, 09:00.
You create a repository of your own, write three lines about your teaching into it, copy it to your laptop and make one commit there. On Friday you bring the file with your three lines into the shared workshop repository with a pull request. The hands-on part of the workshop builds on this step.
You need Steps 3 to 5 first: GitHub Desktop is installed and signed in, and you have accepted the invitation to the organisation gitforsci-rdc.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 1: Create the repository (in the browser)
text:
Part 1: Create the repository (in the browser)

Open https://github.com/new while signed in.
Owner: choose gitforsci-rdc, not your own account.
Repository name: teaching- followed by your GitHub username, for example teaching-octocat.
Choose Private.
Tick Add a README file.
Click Create repository.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 2: Write your three lines (in the browser)
text:
Part 2: Write your three lines (in the browser)

In your new repository, click Add file, then Create new file.
Name the file after your GitHub username with the ending .md, for example octocat.md.
Copy these lines into the file and fill them in:
# your-username

- Who I teach:
- With which tool:
- What blocks me:
Click Commit changes…. Write the commit message Add my teaching context and click Commit changes.

A commit is one saved state of your repository, with who, when and what. You have now made your first one.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 3: Clone the repository (GitHub Desktop)
Clone a repository once. A second click on Clone makes a second copy on your laptop, and the two get mixed up.

Open GitHub Desktop. Choose the menu File, Clone Repository…, then the tab URL.
Type gitforsci-rdc/teaching- followed by your username into the first field.
Look at Local Path. It must end in gitrepos/teaching- followed by your username, in the folder gitrepos you created in Step 5.
Click Clone. GitHub Desktop shows your repository at the top left.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 4: An editor (recommended)
GitHub Desktop shows changes, but it does not edit files. I recommend Sublime Text, a free editor for plain text.

Install Sublime Text.
In GitHub Desktop, open Settings (Windows: File, Options), tab Integrations, and choose Sublime Text as External Editor.

Without Sublime Text, use TextEdit on macOS or Notepad on Windows. Do not use Word.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 5: One commit from your laptop
text:
Part 5: One commit from your laptop

Open the file README.md of your repository. With Sublime Text: menu Repository, Open in Sublime Text, then click README.md. Without it: menu Repository, Show in Finder (Windows: Show in Explorer), then open README.md with TextEdit or Notepad.
Add one sentence below the title, for example what this repository is for. Save the file.
Go back to GitHub Desktop. The tab Changes lists README.md with a tick.
Write a commit message in the field at the bottom left, for example Describe this repository.
Click Commit to main.
Click Push origin at the top. Your commit is now on GitHub as well.

text:
To set up an account on GitHub, follow these general steps:

Go to the GitHub website at https://github.com/.
Click on the “Sign up” button on the top right corner of the page.
Enter your preferred username, email address, and password in the provided fields.
Choose whether you want to receive updates and announcements via email.
Complete the verification process by solving a puzzle and entering a verification code sent to your email.







TipUsername advice from: Happy Git and GitHub for the useR





You will be able to upgrade to a paid level of service, apply discounts, join organizations, etc. in the future, so don’t fret about any of that now. Except your username. You might want to give that some thought.
A few tips, which sadly tend to contradict each other:

Incorporate your actual name! People like to know who they’re dealing with. Also makes your username easier for people to guess or remember.
Reuse your username from other contexts, e.g., Twitter or Slack. But, of course, someone with no GitHub activity will probably be squatting on that.
Pick a username you will be comfortable revealing to your future boss.
Shorter is better than longer.
Be as unique as possible in as few characters as possible. In some settings GitHub auto-completes or suggests usernames.
Make it timeless. Don’t highlight your current university, employer, or place of residence, e.g. JennyFromTheBlock.
Avoid words laden with special meaning in programming.
Avoid the use of upper vs. lower case to separate words. We highly recommend all lowercase. GitHub treats usernames in a case insensitive way, but using all lowercase is kinder to people doing downstream regular expression work with usernames, in various languages. A better strategy for word separation is to use a hyphen -.

You can change your username later, but better to get this right the first time.

https://help.github.com/articles/changing-your-github-username/
https://help.github.com/articles/what-happens-when-i-change-my-username/




Once you have created your GitHub account, enter the username in the pre-course survey if you have not done so yet, or send it to me by email: lschoebitz@ethz.ch. I then invite you to the GitHub organisation for the course.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Background
Git and GitHub are the connective tissue of reproducible, collaborative research, yet many researchers learn them through fragmented tutorials that stop short of the collaboration patterns that matter: branching, pull requests, review and merging. This workshop is delivered as if every participant were a learner, and the real audience is educators: data stewards, research software engineers and instructors who teach, or want to teach, similar material. You first experience a condensed version of the full course from the learner’s seat, then switch to an educator lens to judge whether you could teach it in your own context. The course is published as an open educational resource.

title: Glossary
text:
These are the words you meet in the pre-course work and in the workshop. Each term comes with a short explanation, the place where you see it on your screen, and the Git command behind it.
The workshop runs in GitHub Desktop. Every button there makes Git run a command. The column Command names that command, for the day you work in a terminal or in another tool. Where it says “none”, there is no Git command: the step exists only on the website github.com.

title: Glossary
text:
Git and GitHub









Term
What it means
Where you see it
Command




Branch
A branch is a line of work of your own inside a repository. You change files on it without touching main. When someone has read the changes, they go into main.
GitHub Desktop: Current Branch at the top, then New Branch.
git branch, git switch


Clone
To clone is to copy a whole repository from GitHub to your laptop, with its history and the connection back to GitHub. You clone a repository once and then work in that folder.
GitHub Desktop: menu File, Clone Repository…
git clone


Commit
A commit is one saved state of your repository. Git records the content of your files at that moment, with who saved it, when, and a message that says what changed. You can go back to any earlier commit.
GitHub Desktop: Commit to main at the bottom left. On github.com: Commit changes.
git commit -m "message"


Commit message
The commit message is the short note that goes with a commit. It tells you and others later what changed and why.
GitHub Desktop: the field Summary at the bottom left.
the text after -m


Diff
A diff shows what changed between two versions of a file, one line at a time. Removed lines are red with a minus, new lines are green with a plus.
GitHub Desktop: the right half of the tab Changes. On github.com: the tab Files changed of a pull request.
git diff


Fetch
Fetch asks GitHub whether there are new commits. It does not change your files. When there is something new, the button changes to Pull origin.
GitHub Desktop: Fetch origin at the top.
git fetch


Fork
A fork is your own copy of another person’s repository, stored in your GitHub account. You do not need one in this workshop: you create your branch in the shared repository.
On github.com: Fork at the top right of a repository.
none


History
The history is the list of all commits of a repository, from the first to the latest. It shows who changed what, and when. Every copy of the repository holds the whole history.
GitHub Desktop: the tab History. On github.com: the link commits above the file list.
git log


Issue
An issue is an entry on the GitHub page of a repository for a task, a question or an error. It has a number and stays open until someone closes it. Your pre-work checklist is an issue.
On github.com: the tab Issues.
none


Local
Local means on your laptop. Your local repository is the folder you cloned. You can work and commit in it without an internet connection.
GitHub Desktop: Local Path in the window Clone a Repository.



main
main is the default branch of a repository, the version that counts as the current one. In the workshop, changes reach main through a pull request.
GitHub Desktop: Current Branch shows main.



Merge
To merge is to bring the changes of one branch into another branch. In the workshop, the merge happens when the reviewer accepts a pull request on GitHub.
On github.com: Merge pull request.
git merge


Merge conflict
A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file in different ways. Git stops, marks both versions in the file and waits for your decision. This is not an error.
GitHub Desktop: a notice during the merge. On github.com: Resolve conflicts.



Organisation
An organisation is a shared space on GitHub where repositories belong to a group and not to one person. The workshop has one, and your invitation brings you in. GitHub spells it “organization”.
On github.com: the invitation email with the button Join.
none


origin
origin is the name your local repository uses for its copy on GitHub. Git gives this name when you clone. That is why the buttons read Push origin and Fetch origin.
GitHub Desktop: in Push origin, Pull origin and Fetch origin.
git remote -v


Pull
Pull brings new commits from GitHub into the copy on your laptop.
GitHub Desktop: Pull origin at the top, after Fetch origin.
git pull


Pull request
A pull request is a request on GitHub to read the changes of a branch and to bring them into another branch, most often main. It is a conversation about changes. It exists on GitHub only, not in Git.
GitHub Desktop: Preview Pull Request, after you published your branch. On github.com: the tab Pull requests.
none


Push
Push copies your commits from your laptop to GitHub. Until you push, nobody else sees your commits, and GitHub holds no copy of them.
GitHub Desktop: Push origin at the top.
git push


README
The README is a text file, README.md, that explains what a repository holds and how to use it. GitHub shows it below the file list, so it is the first thing a visitor reads.
On github.com: below the file list. In your folder: the file README.md.



Remote
Remote means on a server and not on your laptop. The remote repository is the copy on GitHub. Your local repository calls it origin.
On github.com: the page of your repository.
git remote -v


Repository
A repository is a folder whose history Git records: all files and every commit ever made. Most often, one project is one repository. After you clone, your repository exists twice, on your laptop and on GitHub.
GitHub Desktop: Current Repository at the top left. On github.com: the page of a repository.



Review
A review is the reading of a pull request by a second person. The reviewer looks at each changed line, writes comments on single lines and ends with a verdict: a comment, a request for changes or an approval.
On github.com: pull request, tab Files changed, button Review changes.
none


Stage
Before a commit you choose which changed files go into it. This is called staging. In GitHub Desktop it is the tick in front of each file.
GitHub Desktop: the ticks in the tab Changes.
git add


Version control
Version control means to record the versions of your files, so that you find every earlier version again and see what changed between two versions. Git is a programme for this.

title: Glossary
section: Buttons and tabs in GitHub Desktop
text:
Buttons and tabs in GitHub Desktop









Label
What it means
Where you see it
Command




Changes
The tab Changes lists every file that changed since the last commit. On the right it shows the diff of the file you clicked. When the list is empty, there is nothing to commit.
Tab at the top left.
git status


Current Branch
The button shows the branch you are on. A click opens the list of branches and the button New Branch. Look here before you commit.
Button at the top, in the middle.
git branch


Current Repository
GitHub Desktop shows one repository at a time. This button names it. A click opens the list of all repositories on your laptop that GitHub Desktop knows.
Button at the top left.



Local Path
Local Path is the folder on your laptop into which GitHub Desktop puts the repository when you clone it. In the workshop it ends in gitrepos, followed by the name of the repository.
Window Clone a Repository.



Publish branch
A new branch exists on your laptop only. Publish branch pushes it to GitHub for the first time, with all its commits. After that the button reads Push origin again.
Button at the top right, in the place of Push origin.
git push -u origin name


Private and Public
When you create a repository, you choose who can see it. Public means everyone on the internet can read it. Private means you and the people who were given access.
On github.com: the page Create a new repository.
none

title: Glossary
text:
The tools







Tool
What it is




Git
Git is a programme on your laptop that records the versions of your files. It saves the versions you tell it to save, shows what changed between two of them and takes you back to any earlier one. Git needs no internet. GitHub Desktop brings Git along, so you do not install it yourself.


GitHub
GitHub is a website, github.com, that holds a copy of your repository on the internet, so that others can see your project and work on it with you. GitHub adds what Git does not have: pull requests, reviews, issues and organisations.


GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop is a programme by GitHub for macOS and Windows. It offers the daily Git steps as buttons: clone, see changes, commit, push, change branches. Every button is a Git command.


Terminal
The terminal is a window in which you type commands as text and do not click buttons. Every button in GitHub Desktop has a command there, for example git push. You do not need the terminal in this workshop.


Editor
An editor is a programme in which you write plain text and code, for example Sublime Text, VS Code or Positron. GitHub Desktop shows changes, and it does not edit files. You edit in the editor and commit in GitHub Desktop.


Markdown
Markdown is plain text with a few characters that GitHub shows as formatting: # at the start of a line for a heading, - for a list. Files that end in .md are Markdown, the README among them.

title: Glossary
text:
Words that get mixed up

Git and GitHub. Git is the programme on your laptop that records the versions of your files. GitHub is the website that holds a copy and adds the collaboration.
Pull and pull request. Pull brings commits from GitHub to your laptop. A pull request asks a second person to read a branch and merge it. They share a word and nothing else.
Commit and push. A commit saves a version on your laptop. A push copies your commits to GitHub. Until you push, nobody else sees them.
Fetch and pull. Fetch looks whether GitHub has something new. Pull brings it into your files.
GitHub Desktop and Git. GitHub Desktop is a window with buttons that runs Git for you. The same commands exist in the terminal and in editors such as VS Code, Positron and RStudio. What you learn in GitHub Desktop holds everywhere.

title: Glossary
text:
Sources
The explanations of the Git and GitHub terms follow Glosario, the glossary of The Carpentries (CC BY 4.0), in my own words. They are ported from the German course gitklar.

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 4: commit

Go back to GitHub Desktop. The tab Changes lists people/your-username.md with a tick.
Write a message in the field Summary at the bottom left, for example Add my teaching context.
The button below now reads Commit 1 file to people-your-username. If it ends in to main, you are on the wrong branch. Go back to step 2.
Click the button.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
section: Step 5: publish the branch and open the pull request
text:
Step 5: publish the branch and open the pull request
Your branch exists only on your laptop so far.

Click Publish branch at the top. GitHub Desktop pushes the branch with your commit to GitHub.
Click the blue button Preview Pull Request. A window shows your file.
At the top it reads base: main and compare: people-your-username. That is how it should be. Click Create Pull Request at the bottom right. Your browser opens on github.com.
The text field holds a template with two lines. Fill in File with people/your-username.md.
On the right, click Reviewers and type larnsce. Choose the name from the list.
Click the green button Create pull request.

Your pull request is open. Do not merge it yourself, also when GitHub shows you the button. Reading by a second person is the point of the exercise.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 6: review, answer, merge
You are the author of the pull request, Lars is the reviewer.

Lars: writes one question on a line of your file. GitHub sends you a notification by email.
You: open your pull request in the list of pull requests. You see the comment there. Answer it in the file: open Documents/gitrepos/workshop/people/your-username.md in your editor, change the line and save. In GitHub Desktop, write a commit message, click Commit 1 file to people-your-username, then Push origin. The open pull request shows the new commit. You need no second pull request.
Lars: reads your commit and merges the pull request.
You: in GitHub Desktop, click Current Branch and choose main. Click Fetch origin, then Pull origin. The folder people on your laptop now holds the files of everyone who is merged.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Done when
Your pull request stands under closed pull requests with the purple mark Merged, and your file is in the folder people on main.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Stuck?

A commit on main instead of your branch. As long as you have not pushed, GitHub Desktop shows the button Undo at the bottom left, below the commit. Click it. Then create the branch (step 2). GitHub Desktop asks whether your changes should come along. Choose to bring them to the new branch.
Nothing appears in the tab Changes. The file is in a different place. It belongs into gitrepos/workshop/people.
Changes shows a folder instead of one file. You copied the repository folder. Delete the copied folder from workshop/people and copy only the file your-username.md.
The push is rejected. Your commit carries your real email address, and your account blocks such pushes. In GitHub Desktop, open Settings (Windows: File, Options), Git, tab Author, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com and click Save. Then click Undo at the bottom of the tab Changes and commit again.
Publish branch is missing, the top reads Push origin. The branch is published already. Click Push origin if commits are missing and go on with step 5.
The name is not in the list of reviewers. Go on without a reviewer. Lars sees every new pull request in the repository.
Anything else: write a comment in your issue in the workshop repository.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request
